difficultyReason: Requires integrating the adherence statistic with the subgroup finding to infer a hedged claim about adherence, not a blanket claim about the diet's efficacy. Trap (A) overreaches on efficacy; trap (D) inverts the direction.
stimulus: A recent clinical trial assigned patients with elevated cholesterol either to a plant-based diet or to a standard low-fat diet. Across the full sample, average cholesterol levels dropped by similar amounts in both groups. However, fewer than half of the patients assigned to the plant-based diet reported sticking to it for the full twelve weeks, while the overwhelming majority of patients on the standard diet reported complying. Among patients who reported full adherence, those on the plant-based diet showed markedly greater reductions than those on the standard diet.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plant-based diet is the most effective dietary intervention available for patients with elevated cholesterol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients who would benefit substantially from a plant-based diet are unlikely to follow it long enough to do so.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients assigned to a standard low-fat diet will always report higher rates of adherence than those assigned to a plant-based diet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dietary interventions are generally less effective at reducing cholesterol than medication-based interventions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The standard low-fat diet is as effective as the plant-based diet when both are followed consistently.

explanations.correct: Two facts combine to support (B): fewer than half of plant-based patients adhered, and among those who did, reductions were markedly greater. So at least some patients who would have benefited substantially did not stick with it. The hedged 'at least some' is well within what the data support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'most effective available' makes a superlative claim well beyond a two-arm comparison.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'will always' extrapolates a single trial's adherence pattern into an absolute rule.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about medication.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the adherent-subgroup data show the plant-based diet produced markedly greater reductions, not equal ones.

difficultyReason: Must integrate the earnings comparison with the hours datapoint to reach a hedged productivity-per-hour claim. Trap (E) overreaches to all drivers; trap (B) confuses the direction of the earnings comparison.
stimulus: A survey of rideshare drivers in several large metropolitan areas found that drivers who work primarily during weekday commuting hours earn, on average, roughly the same total weekly income as drivers who work primarily on weekend evenings. The commuting-hour drivers, however, spend on average about 25 percent more hours logged into the rideshare application per week than the weekend-evening drivers do.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most rideshare drivers prefer working weekend evenings to working weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weekend-evening drivers earn less per week than weekday commuting-hour drivers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some rideshare drivers earn more per hour logged into the application on weekend evenings than they would during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rideshare passengers tip more generously on weekend evenings than during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any driver who switches from weekday commuting hours to weekend evenings will increase his or her total weekly income.

explanations.correct: Similar total weekly income combined with substantially fewer logged-in hours implies a higher per-hour rate, at least on average, for weekend-evening drivers. 'Some drivers earn more per hour' is a hedged claim that follows cleanly from these two facts.
explanations.A: Out of scope — preferences aren't discussed.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — total weekly incomes are described as roughly equal, not lower for weekend drivers.
explanations.D: Unsupported — tipping is one possible source of the earnings pattern, but the stimulus doesn't establish it.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'any driver' switching guarantees no increase in earnings; the data describe averages, not individuals.

difficultyReason: Combines the restoration outcome with the species-specific exception to support a hedged claim about restoration's limits. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) drops the qualifier about what drainage accomplishes.
stimulus: When drained wetlands in the coastal region of Ferndale were re-flooded as part of a restoration program, populations of most native waterbird species rebounded to levels comparable to those recorded before drainage. One species, the banded bittern, had nested almost exclusively in a particular type of dense reed bed that had grown up during the decades of drainage. Ten years after re-flooding, banded bittern numbers in Ferndale remain less than half their pre-drainage levels.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetland restoration programs are generally ineffective at reviving native bird populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The banded bittern is in greater need of conservation attention than any other waterbird in Ferndale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Re-flooding drained wetlands is not by itself sufficient to restore every native bird species that was historically present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drainage of wetlands typically benefits the bird species that inhabit them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reed beds that grew during drainage are more valuable habitat than the original wetlands were.

explanations.correct: Most species rebounded after re-flooding, but the banded bittern did not — it depended on reed beds that only emerged during drainage. This supports the hedged claim that re-flooding alone is not sufficient for every species. 'Not sufficient' is exactly the language MSS favors.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — most species rebounded, which is evidence restoration is generally effective.
explanations.B: Unsupported — relative conservation priority is not established by the stimulus.
explanations.D: Too strong and opposite — 'typically benefits' overreaches from one species' dependence on reed beds to a general claim about drainage.
explanations.E: Too strong — one species' preference doesn't show the reed beds are more valuable overall.

difficultyReason: Integrates the borrowing pattern with the timing observation to support a hedged inference about cultural contact. Trap (B) overreaches on causation; trap (E) scope-creeps from maritime terms to the whole lexicon.
stimulus: The Kaldari language contains dozens of words for types of sails, fishing equipment, and navigational landmarks that are clearly borrowed from Old Merenni, the language of a now-vanished seafaring people who lived along a coast several hundred miles to the south. By contrast, Kaldari retains no Merenni-derived words for agriculture, food preparation, or family relations. Linguists have dated the borrowed maritime terms to a period roughly a century before the first written records of regular trade between the two peoples.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speakers of Kaldari had some maritime contact with Merenni speakers before trade between the two peoples was formally recorded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Merenni people taught the Kaldari most of what they knew about sailing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two peoples had no significant cultural contact of any kind prior to the period of recorded trade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kaldari speakers borrowed words only from languages of peoples they encountered through trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Kaldari vocabulary was shaped by contact with the Merenni.

explanations.correct: Borrowed maritime terms predating the first records of regular trade support an inference that some maritime contact existed before the recorded trade period. The hedged 'some' fits the data well.
explanations.B: Too strong — borrowing vocabulary is evidence of contact, not of being taught 'most' of what one knows.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — the borrowed terms are themselves evidence of some prior contact.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'only' rules out all other sources of borrowing without support.
explanations.E: Scope creep — dozens of maritime terms aren't 'most' of the vocabulary.

difficultyReason: Must connect the coin-distribution pattern with the absence of a local mint to support a hedged trade-route inference. Trap (C) overreaches from 'some' contact to 'primary'; trap (D) inverts the natural inference.
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a twelfth-century settlement in the inland region of Arvath have uncovered coins minted in the distant port of Daemos, in quantities comparable to those found at sites along the well-documented Daemos–Arvath trade road. Daemos coins have also been found in smaller quantities at several sites along a mountain pass route that historians had previously assumed was used only for seasonal herding. No mint is known to have operated in Arvath itself during the twelfth century.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the Daemos coins found at the mountain-pass sites arrived there through commercial exchange rather than seasonal herding alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mountain pass route was used more heavily for trade than the well-documented Daemos–Arvath road was.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daemos was the primary source of currency for inland Arvath during the twelfth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arvath produced its own coins but did so secretly to avoid Daemos's influence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Daemos–Arvath trade road fell out of regular use during the twelfth century.

explanations.correct: Coins from a distant port turning up along a pass route previously thought to serve only herding supports a hedged inference that at least some exchange occurred along that route — consistent with coins being a standard indicator of commerce.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the pass sites show smaller quantities than the road sites.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'primary source' is a superlative claim not supported by the quantities alone.
explanations.D: Directly contradicted — no mint is known to have operated in Arvath.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the road sites still show trade-road-level coin quantities.

difficultyReason: Combines the reuse statistic with the breach-source data to support a hedged claim about password managers as insufficient rather than harmful. Trap (A) inverts; trap (D) overreaches on a tool's sufficiency.
stimulus: A survey of corporate employees found that those who regularly used a password manager were significantly less likely to reuse the same password across multiple work accounts than those who did not. Nonetheless, a study of recent security breaches at the same companies found that employees who used password managers accounted for nearly as large a share of breached accounts as those who did not. In most of these breaches, the point of compromise was a phishing attack rather than a guessed or stolen password.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Password managers tend to make corporate accounts less secure overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate employees who use password managers are no more cautious about phishing attempts than their coworkers who do not use such tools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phishing attacks are the most common cause of password reuse in corporate settings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adopting a password manager is sufficient to protect an employee from the most common forms of account compromise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Companies would experience fewer breaches if they banned the use of password managers.

explanations.correct: If managers reduce reuse but breach rates stay comparable — and most breaches are phishing-based — then use of a manager doesn't correspond to a lower phishing-compromise rate. That supports the hedged claim that manager users are no more cautious about phishing than non-users.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the data don't show managers make things worse; they show they don't help against phishing in particular.
explanations.C: Category error — phishing causes breaches in this data, not password reuse.
explanations.D: Too strong, and the stimulus supports the opposite (managers don't prevent phishing-based compromise).
explanations.E: Opposite direction — a ban would restore password reuse, which the stimulus implies managers reduce.

difficultyReason: Integrates the recording constraint with the soloist behavior to support a hedged inference about early jazz conventions. Trap (B) creeps to 'any recording'; trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth not anchored in the facts.
stimulus: In the early days of commercial jazz recording, a single side of a 78-rpm disc could hold only about three minutes of music, far less than the typical length of a live jazz performance. Historians have observed that recordings made in this period contain noticeably fewer and shorter instrumental solos than eyewitness accounts describe as typical of the same ensembles' live performances. Several prominent soloists of the period complained in print that the recording format forced them to omit material they considered essential to their playing.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The recording format of the era probably shaped the form in which some early jazz solos have been preserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any recording made during this period misrepresents the ensemble that produced it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live jazz performances of the era were always substantially longer than three minutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most jazz soloists of the period preferred live performance to studio recording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Technological constraints have generally done more to shape music than to preserve it.

explanations.correct: The length limit, the gap between recordings and live accounts, and the soloists' own complaints together support the hedged inference that the format shaped what was preserved. 'Probably' and 'some' fit the level of warrant.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any recording misrepresents' overreaches from 'fewer and shorter solos' to universal misrepresentation.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'always' and 'substantially' overreach the word 'typical.'
explanations.D: Unsupported — preference between media isn't established.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported worldly generalization — the stimulus speaks only to a specific case.

difficultyReason: Must combine the checkout decline with the program-use rise to support a hedged inference about library function. Trap (A) inverts; trap (C) extends from 'at least one' to 'most.'
stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of books checked out from the public library system of Porthaven has fallen by more than a third. During the same period, however, the total number of people who use at least one library facility in a given month has grown substantially, and library programs that do not involve borrowing books — such as tax-preparation clinics, job-search workshops, and children's story hours — have seen sharp increases in attendance.
questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Porthaven are reading fewer books than they did a decade ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some Porthaven residents now rely on the library primarily for services other than borrowing books.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who visit the Porthaven library no longer check out any books at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The library system would attract even more users if it stopped offering non-book programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public libraries in other cities are experiencing trends similar to those in Porthaven.

explanations.correct: Total monthly users have grown substantially while checkouts have fallen, and non-borrowing programs have grown sharply. That combination supports the hedged claim that at least some residents now rely on the library primarily for non-book services.
explanations.A: Unsupported — people can read books obtained from sources other than the library (bookstores, e-books, etc.).
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most' visitors no longer checking out anything goes beyond what declining-but-still-substantial checkouts can support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — non-book programs are correlated with rising usage.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus addresses only Porthaven.

difficultyReason: Integrates the sleep recommendation, the self-report finding, and the device data to support a hedged claim about under- rather than over-estimation of sleep. Trap (D) overreaches to the clinical category; trap (A) is the opposite.
stimulus: Health authorities generally recommend that adults sleep between seven and nine hours each night. In a recent large survey, a majority of respondents reported that they typically slept less than the recommended amount. A subsequent study of participants who wore sleep-tracking devices for several weeks, however, found that nearly half of those who had earlier reported getting less than seven hours of sleep were in fact averaging more than seven hours per night according to the devices.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sleep-tracking devices systematically overstate the amount of time their users spend asleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of adults who actually sleep fewer than seven hours per night may be smaller than survey results have suggested.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most adults who believe themselves to be sleep-deprived are in fact getting adequate sleep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adult sleep deprivation is not a genuine health concern.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People who use sleep-tracking devices tend to sleep longer than people who do not.

explanations.correct: If nearly half of self-reported under-sleepers were actually averaging more than seven hours, the survey-based picture probably overstates the number of adults sleeping too little. 'May be smaller' is appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't say devices overstate; it says self-report and device data diverge, with no basis to privilege self-report.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most adults who believe themselves sleep-deprived' overreaches from 'nearly half of one subgroup.'
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus doesn't dismiss the concern, only suggests its magnitude may be overstated.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't compare device users to non-users.

difficultyReason: Connects the larval-survival datapoint with the protection-status contrast to support a hedged inference about the role of reserve size. Trap (A) overreaches on reserves' general effectiveness; trap (E) is a plausible worldly claim not anchored in the stimulus.
stimulus: Marine biologists studying a coral reef system have found that the abundance of several commercially valuable fish species is substantially higher inside small protected reserves than in adjacent unprotected waters. Larvae of these species, however, drift on ocean currents for weeks before settling, and genetic analyses indicate that larvae produced within the reserves are regularly carried far beyond reserve boundaries. In nearby reef systems where no reserves have been established, populations of the same species have continued to decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Small marine reserves are sufficient to halt the decline of commercially valuable fish species throughout any reef system in which they are established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some populations of commercially valuable fish outside small marine reserves benefit from the existence of those reserves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larval dispersal is the main factor determining fish abundance within marine reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most commercial fishers prefer to fish just outside the boundaries of marine reserves.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding existing marine reserves would produce proportionally greater benefits for fish populations.

explanations.correct: Reserves contain more abundant populations; larvae produced there regularly drift beyond the boundaries; and unprotected reef systems without reserves continue to decline. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some outside populations benefit from the reserves. 'Some' is the right level of warrant.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'sufficient to halt decline throughout any reef system' overreaches from localized abundance findings.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'the main factor' is a superlative not supported by the stimulus.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported — proportionality of benefits isn't established.
